issues.legal_issue: A lease made in breach of statutory letting requirements is not void or unenforceable between landlord and tenant unless the governing law expressly invalidates the agreement.
material_facts: The landlord let the building to a tenant without an allotment order.
The tenant paid rent for three months and then stopped paying; the trial court found the rent and default proved but dismissed the ejectment suit solely because the letting contravened the Act.
The landlord challenged the dismissal, and the Full Bench had held that the agreement was void and unenforceable.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was not void merely because the letting contravened the Act. Unless the statute specifically provides that a contract contrary to it is void, the contract remains binding between the parties and may be enforced between them. The High Court’s contrary ruling was set aside, and the writ petition was remanded for decision in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Nanakram v. Kundalrai, (1986) 3 SCC 83, absent a mandatory statutory provision requiring eviction or declaring the agreement void, the parties remain bound by their agreement as between themselves. The Court held that Waman Shriniwas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co., (1959) Supp. 2 SCR 217, concerned an express statutory prohibition on subletting and was consistent with Nanakram; Sri Krishna Khanna v. A.D.M., Kanpur, (1975) 2 SCC 361, concerned the public authority’s power to allot despite an agreement between the parties; and Mannalal Khetan v. Kedar Nath Khetan, (1977) 2 SCC 424, concerned an agreement contrary to company-law provisions and attachment orders. Those cases did not displace Nanakram. The relevant statutory context included Sections 11, 13, 17 and 31 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972; the Full Bench’s reliance on Sections 10 and 23 of the Contract Act did not justify disregarding Nanakram.

predicates.landlord_tenant_contract_dispute: A landlord and tenant are disputing the effect or enforcement of their agreement.
predicates.lease_breaches_regulatory_requirement: The landlord let the premises in a way that did not comply with a regulatory requirement governing the letting.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_invalidate_contra: The governing law prohibits the noncompliant transaction but does not expressly make the agreement void.

issues.definition: When a landlord and tenant dispute an agreement made in breach of a regulatory requirement, and the governing law does not expressly invalidate it, the agreement remains enforceable between them.

issues.legal_issue: An ejectment suit may be brought to recover possession from an occupant whom the governing law treats as unauthorised for occupying without the required allotment, independently of the letting agreement.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the building under a letting made without an allotment order.
The landlord brought an ejectment suit, which the trial court dismissed on the ground that the letting agreement contravened the Act.
The Act treated a person occupying without an allotment or release order as an unauthorised occupant.
issues.conclusion: A suit to eject an unauthorised occupant and recover possession may be brought independently of the contract; such a suit is not barred as an action founded on the noncompliant agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 deems a person occupying without an allotment or release order to be an unauthorised occupant. The Court reasoned that an action to recover possession from such an occupant is an action against a trespasser, not an action founded on the parties’ agreement, and is therefore not barred on that basis.

predicates.ejectment_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking to eject an occupant from premises.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession_from_occupant: The landlord seeks to recover possession from the person occupying the premises.
predicates.occupant_lacks_required_allotment_or_rel: The occupant entered or remained in occupation without the order required by the governing law.

issues.definition: An ejectment suit is maintainable when a landlord seeks possession from an occupant who lacks the order required for occupation.

issues.legal_issue: A lower court must follow a binding higher-court decision that directly resolves the legal issue before it when the decisions said to conflict address distinct questions.
material_facts: A Full Bench considered whether a lease made in breach of statutory letting requirements was void and enforceable.
The Supreme Court had already directly addressed those questions in a binding decision.
The Full Bench regarded other Supreme Court decisions as conflicting, but those decisions concerned distinct legal questions.
issues.conclusion: The Full Bench was bound to follow the directly applicable Supreme Court authority and was not entitled to take a contrary view; the decisions it cited did not create a conflict on the question decided in that authority.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied judicial discipline and the binding force of Supreme Court precedent. It held that Nanakram v. Kundalrai, (1986) 3 SCC 83, directly decided the relevant questions and bound the Full Bench. Waman Shriniwas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co., (1959) Supp. 2 SCR 217, Sri Krishna Khanna v. A.D.M., Kanpur, (1975) 2 SCC 361, and Mannalal Khetan v. Kedar Nath Khetan, (1977) 2 SCC 424, addressed different issues and were not contrary authorities on those questions.

predicates.lower_court_is_resolving_legal_issue: A lower court is deciding a legal issue in a case before it.
predicates.binding_higher_court_authority_directly_: A binding decision of a higher court has directly resolved the same legal issue.
predicates.purportedly_conflicting_decisions_addres: Other decisions said to conflict address legal questions distinct from the issue already resolved.

issues.definition: A lower court must follow a binding higher-court decision that directly resolves the issue when the decisions said to conflict address distinct questions.
